description_full: Northrop Grumman Corporation operates as an aerospace and defense technology company in the United States, Asia/Pacific, Europe, and internationally. It operates through four segments: Aeronautics Systems, Defense Systems, Mission Systems and Space Systems. The Aeronautics Systems segment designs, develops, produces, integrates, sustains, and modernizes aircraft systems. This segment also offers unmanned autonomous aircraft systems, including high-altitude long-endurance strategic, surveillance and reconnaissance systems; and strategic long-range strike aircraft, tactical fighter and air dominance aircraft, and airborne battle management and command and control systems. Its Defense Systems segment designs, develops, integrates, and produces strategic deterrent systems, tactical weapons, and missile defense solutions; and provides sustainment, modernization, and training services for manned and unmanned aircraft and electronics systems. This segment also offers strategic missiles; integrated all-domain command and control systems; precision strike weapons; tactical solid rocket motors, and high-speed air-breathing and hypersonic systems; high-performance gun systems, ammunition, precision munitions, and advanced fuzes; and sustainment, operation, and modernization. The Mission Systems segment provides command, control, communication and computer, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance systems; radar, electro-optical/infrared, and acoustic sensors; electronic warfare systems; advanced communications and network systems; microelectronics; navigation and positioning sensors; maritime power, propulsion, and payload launch systems; cyber solutions; and intelligence processing systems. Its Space Systems segment offers satellites, spacecraft systems, subsystems, sensors, and payloads; ground systems; missile defense systems and interceptors; and launch vehicles and related propulsion systems. The company was founded in 1939 and is based in Falls Church, Virginia.

financial_summary: Northrop Grumman Corporation is a large-cap industrials business with a $78.2B market cap on $42.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 13% against a 7% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $3.3B in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.14× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 6.8×.

Shareholder yield of 3.7% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 11% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).

mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 12% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 29% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.45, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $447.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 30% in the 2020 crash, 12% in the 2022 bear market and 58% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $532 (margin of safety -3%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 5%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $407 to $719 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 17.4 vs 24.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 54% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 24 covering analysts target $635 on average, 15% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 13% earns above the cost of capital of 7.0%, but the 6pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.14x.
ROE of 25% is amplified by 3.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 2.6% of revenue on R&D and 0.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.9x net debt to EBITDA ($4.4B of cash against $15.7B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.8x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.7% over 3 years, 2.7% over 5 years and 6.0% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 33% of profits supports about 4.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 2.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.10 (orders outpacing sales) and a backlog worth 2.3x annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 3.5% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 10, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and institutions hold 83%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (27 sales, net $811K sold).
It returns 3.7% a year to shareholders (2.1% in buybacks and 1.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 44 consecutive years, raising it 6.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 95,000 employees, each generates about $442K of revenue, 1.2x the Industrials median.
That works out to $35K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $7.3M (17x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
